messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Arjun Patel is a 35-year-old tax consultant who came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was “just tired” and that work stress was catching up with him. Before returning to the U.S., he had spent several weeks as a relief worker in a war zone, helping distribute supplies and assisting with evacuations after shelling in a civilian area. The moment that now sits at the center of his distress is fragmented in his telling: he remembers smoke hanging low over a damaged street, people shouting, and moving toward a building where families had been sheltering. He recalls seeing bodies brought out, the air thick with burning and dust, and being forced to choose who could be moved first. A burial area had formed nearby because there was nowhere else to take the dead. What stays with him most is the conviction that others were looking to him and that he did not do enough.

Since returning home, seemingly ordinary moments in his daily life as a tax consultant have become charged with danger. If he passes a cluster of smokers outside his office building, the smell of smoke catches in his throat and his whole body reacts before he can think. If a client raises their voice in irritation, even calmly, he feels himself tense and brace. When a colleague mentioned attending a funeral for her father, he had to leave the break room. These moments do not stay small. The smell, the word funeral, the sight of anger on someone’s face immediately pull up pieces of the war-zone scene, and he can suddenly feel his body folding into the same protective crouch he had taken there, his hands drawn up toward his face as if shielding himself.

The memories come in a disjointed way that unsettles him further. He cannot place what happened in a clear sequence, only broken images and bodily sensations. At night, when the house is quiet, he finds it harder to feel safe than during the day; the dark seems to leave too much room for something to happen. Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming outside, the heating system clicking on—make him jump sharply, and afterwards the half-formed memories push closer. In those moments he is not only remembering smoke and shouted instructions; he is flooded with shame, gripped by the sense that he had been in the position to protect people and failed.

That meaning has spread far beyond the event itself. Arjun has come to believe that the world no longer works according to any dependable rules, that catastrophe can arrive without warning and that decency offers no protection. He feels cut off from other people, including friends who try to welcome him back into normal routines. When triggers hit—a funeral notice online, smoke from a neighbor’s grill, a flash of irritation in someone’s voice—they do not just evoke memory; they confirm what he now believes about himself and the world. He hears in another person’s anger the same helpless urgency of those days overseas, and he reads his own reaction as proof that he is fundamentally different from everyone around him.

Over time he has organized his life around trying not to feel any of this. He avoids the part of the city where a humanitarian fundraiser was held because it reminds him of the field site and the people he could not save. When something upsetting catches him off guard, he covers his face with his hands, a gesture that briefly blocks the room around him but also puts him back into the body posture of the event. He has also begun turning away from invitations that might make him feel good—his wife’s plans for dinners out, celebrations with cousins, even a weekend trip—because hope and pleasure feel almost disloyal. If he lets himself enjoy anything, he fears he is erasing the dead or excusing his failure. These habits have narrowed his life, and in the narrowing he feels even more separate and ashamed.

The strategies that are meant to keep him steady seem instead to tighten everything. Avoiding reminders leaves the memories more confused and jagged, never fully sorted into the past. Covering his face when distressed makes the bodily sense of the event more immediate. Staying away from happy occasions has strained his marriage; his wife experiences him as absent and unreachable, which he silently takes as further evidence that he does not belong with other people anymore. At work, his concentration has worsened during client meetings, especially late in the day or after being startled by a noise in the office, and he has become increasingly vigilant by evening, checking locks and scanning sounds outside the apartment.

What finally brought Arjun in was a recent family funeral. He had agreed to attend for the sake of his parents, but the smell of incense and cremation smoke, the gathered grief, and a relative’s curt voice sent him spiraling into a familiar collapse of body memory, shame, and alarm. He spent much of the service with his face in his hands, then left abruptly and sat in his car shaking. He told his wife afterward that he was afraid he was becoming someone who could no longer live in ordinary life—someone always waiting for the next sign of danger, always one reminder away from that street. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is not to forget what happened, but to be able to remember it without feeling condemned by it.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show Arjun’s negative appraisals causing him to become more sensitive to or generate triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat and alarm occurring alongside shame and beliefs, but it does not explicitly convey that his sense of threat leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly state that Arjun’s sense of threat increases attention to, sensitivity to, or creation of triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Although avoidance and other maladaptive strategies are described as narrowing his life, the vignette does not clearly state that these strategies lead to increased exposure to or sensitivity to triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies maintaining memories and shame, but it does not explicitly convey that these strategies heighten Arjun’s sense of threat or danger.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That meaning has spread far beyond the event itself. Arjun has come to believe that the world no longer works according to any dependable rules, that catastrophe can arrive without warning and that decency offers no protection.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Holding that belief, he moved through ordinary days as if they were full of signals he could not afford to miss; a raised voice in the office, smoke on someone’s clothes, even the mention of a funeral snagged his attention as possible signs that the same kind of catastrophe was close again.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Ordinary sounds—a car door slamming outside, the heating system clicking on—make him jump sharply, and afterwards the half-formed memories push closer.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that pitch of alarm gradually convinced him that his fear was telling the truth: that he was no longer someone who could count on safety, and that ordinary life itself had become precarious.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At work, his concentration has worsened during client meetings, especially late in the day or after being startled by a noise in the office, and he has become increasingly vigilant by evening, checking locks and scanning sounds outside the apartment.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Already braced for danger, he found that more and more of the world registered as warning; by the end of a workday, ambiguous noises in the hallway, a stranger lingering near the building entrance, or irritation in a client’s tone could all flare into reminders.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time he has organized his life around trying not to feel any of this.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Those efforts ended up drawing the boundaries of the trauma through his week: the streets he no longer took, the conversations he cut short, and the family events he declined all became reminders in their own right, keeping funerals, smoke, and anger continually marked out in his mind.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The strategies that are meant to keep him steady seem instead to tighten everything.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because he so often escaped, covered his face, checked, or stayed away before finding out he was actually safe, his body never had reason to revise its alarm; the very things he did to get through the moment left danger feeling current and unresolved.
<<<END>>>
